name: Sardines / oily fish

image.caption: School of sardines at the Monterey Bay Aquarium (12056)

lead: Sardines are small oily fish eaten fresh, grilled, smoked or canned, valued as an inexpensive source of protein, B12 and omega-3 fats. Some in appearance communities eat them for healthier-looking skin.

The route people point to is omega-3 intake lowering skin inflammation. Canned Pacific sardines provide 375 percent of the daily value of B12 per 100 grams and calcium when eaten with the bones. No clinical studies on sardines for skin were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: People eat canned sardines on toast, with rice or in salads, a few times a week as a budget protein. Canned fish is shelf-stable, which makes it easy to keep up.
Sardines are described as lower in mercury than many fish, and canned versions contain notable sodium. Pacific sardine fisheries have faced closures, which can affect supply.

angle.text: Sardines and other oily fish are eaten as a cheap source of omega-3 fats, B12 and protein, with users linking them to healthier-looking skin through lower inflammation. Omega-3 intake is widely studied for health; skin benefits from eating oily fish were not tested in the sources reviewed.

lead: Sardines and other oily fish such as herring, mackerel, anchovies and salmon are eaten by people who want clearer, calmer skin and a leaner, better-fed physique. Sardines are small, inexpensive and eaten fresh, grilled, smoked or canned. Oily fish are the main dietary source of the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA [1], and canned sardines also supply protein, vitamin B12 and, when the soft bones are eaten, calcium [2]; oily fish as a group are rich in vitamins A and D.

The appearance case rests on two chains. Omega-3 fatty acids partly inhibit several aspects of inflammation in laboratory and clinical research [3][4], and people who follow skin-focused diets cite this as a reason to eat oily fish for a less inflamed complexion. Sardines are also a cheap, high-protein food that fits the diets of people building muscle and losing fat, and T Nation posters mention them as a cheap staple [5].

Health agencies recommend oily fish mainly for general health: the American Heart Association recommends it twice weekly for people without coronary heart disease, the WHO suggests one to two servings of fish weekly, and the EFSA gives an adequate intake of 250 mg per day of EPA plus DHA. No published trial of sardine consumption with skin appearance as the outcome was found.

paras: Per 100 grams, canned Pacific sardines provide about 185 kilocalories, 20.9 grams of protein and 10.4 grams of fat, plus B12, phosphorus, niacin, riboflavin, calcium, iron and zinc [2]. Wikipedia describes oily fish as rich in fat-soluble vitamins A and D and in omega-3 fatty acids, at much higher levels than whitefish such as cod. Fillets of oily fish can hold up to 30 percent oil.

Oily fish are the main dietary source of EPA and DHA, along with salmon, herring, mackerel, anchovies and trout. Reviews describe EPA and DHA as partly inhibiting aspects of inflammation, including white blood cell movement, adhesion molecule expression and production of pro-inflammatory messengers, and giving rise to resolvins that help resolve inflammation [3][4]. Wikipedia reports that marine omega-3 intake lowers blood inflammation markers such as CRP, IL-6 and TNF-alpha. These findings concern inflammation generally; the reviews cited do not test skin appearance.

The American Heart Association recommends oily fish twice weekly for people without coronary heart disease, the WHO recommends one to two fish servings weekly, and the EFSA gives an adequate intake of 250 mg per day of EPA plus DHA for adults. A study paper on omega-3 status notes that UK and EU expert panels recommend about 250 mg EPA and DHA per day, equivalent to one portion of oily fish a week [6]. In the UK a 2004 recommendation was at least two portions of fish weekly, one of them oily.

Because they sit low on the food chain, sardines are described as carrying less mercury than many other commonly eaten fish [2], while oily fish generally can carry higher levels of mercury, dioxins and other pollutants than whitefish. In April 2015 the Pacific Fishery Management Council halted the US West Coast commercial sardine season after stocks collapsed [2]. The IUCN lists the European pilchard as Least Concern [2]. Researchers note that increasing oily fish consumption conflicts with sustaining fisheries and are studying alternatives such as mussels [6].
Cornish pilchard fishing thrived from about 1750 to 1880, and the last large US sardine cannery closed in 2010 [2].

Posters on T Nation mention sardines and pilchards as a cheap, tasty snack and as a way to get omega-3s alongside or instead of fish oil capsules; one poster calls pilchards cheap and tasty [5]. Another thread lists sardines among foods that supply vitamin D [7].

No studies found on sardines specifically for skin or appearance outcomes. Studies of fish consumption have examined the omega-3 index in young adults [8], and reviews cover omega-3 fatty acids and inflammatory processes [3][4].
